title: Who ran it, and who tried to buy it
lede: Ages and titles are as given in the press at the time. Later careers are left out where we have no source.

people.name: Michael J. Vastola
people.text: Joined Lionel in 1971 as a junior accountant and was vice president of finance when it filed in 1982. Named chairman and chief executive in March 1983, aged 37, and led the company out of Chapter 11, through the takeover fight and into the second filing.[^4][^16][^23]

people.name: Leonard Wasserman
people.text: Lionel’s senior vice president for retail. He served as acting president and chief executive of the parent from July 1982 to March 1983, then returned to running the stores subsidiary.[^3][^4]

people.name: Ronald Saypol
people.text: Resigned at 52, with chief operating officer Richard R. Schilling Jr., under pressure from creditors five months into the first bankruptcy.[^3]

people.name: Marvin Katz
people.text: Walked a Times reporter through the new Manhattan store and its 28 registers. Asked by a shopper how many Lazer Tag sets he had, he answered: “I have 98,000.”[^10]

people.name: Neil B. Friedman
people.role: COO of Lionel Leisure from Jun 1991
people.text: A former Hasbro marketing executive, named a director and chief operating officer of the stores subsidiary on the day of the second filing, at 43.[^16][^17]

people.name: George A. Padgett
people.role: Senior vice president and general counsel
people.text: The company’s spokesman through the takeover fight and the second bankruptcy. In June 1992 he said the remaining stores were profitable.[^12][^20]

people.name: Robert I. Toussie
people.text: A New York real estate developer, 48 at the time, whose partnership held 9.9% of Lionel and offered $8.25 a share. He dropped the bid in January 1990 after a $500,000 settlement.[^11][^12][^14]

people.name: Richard P. Kughn
people.text: A Detroit real estate developer and train collector who bought the train business in 1986. His company bought the Lionel trademarks from the retailer in 1990.[^9][^16]
people.later: Told the Los Angeles Times in 1990 that train sales had tripled in four years to $60M.[^31]
